claims.text: Chemically distinct, structurally coherent interfaces in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings act as effective dislocation barriers.
Multilayer interfaces promote local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering increases lattice friction to dislocation motion.
The combined interface and local-ordering barriers reduce creep relative to a homogeneous single-phase coating.
Alternating chemically distinct high-entropy-alloy layers with well-defined interfaces can be fabricated by arc ion plating.
Alternating chemically distinct high-entropy-alloy layers with well-defined interfaces can be fabricated by spark deposition.
A multilayer coating and a homogeneous single-layer coating can be prepared with identical overall composition for a controlled comparison.
Sustained high temperature and moderate mechanical loading promote time-dependent plastic deformation by creep.
Local chemical ordering is present specifically in regions at the multilayer interfaces.
Interfacial misfit stresses hinder dislocation motion under applied stress.
Local chemical ordering raises activation barriers for dislocation nucleation and glide.
Interface-induced barriers slow the accumulation of plastic strain over time.
Under identical temperature and load, the multilayer coating will have significantly lower creep strain than the homogeneous coating.
Under identical temperature and load, the multilayer coating will show a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to the homogeneous coating.
The proposed resistance mechanism applies only while multilayer interfaces remain structurally stable.
Interfacial degradation or phase transformation at sufficiently high temperature or stress will remove the proposed applicability of the mechanism.
The mechanism requires sufficiently chemically distinct and coherent layers.
The relative contributions of interface barriers and intrinsic bulk high-entropy-alloy properties, and their variation among alloy systems, remain unquantified.
